title: Friends, I'm officially calling it: algorithmic trading is entering a new era.
author: EAForexLab
selftext:
Today, an AI agent independently optimized a trading EA in MT5, analyzed the results, and performed cross-validation.

All on its own, without any involvement from me. While I was at the gym.

Were there some issues with the results? Absolutely. But here's the exciting part: many of them can be addressed by refining the prompts and improving the agent's workflow.

Not long ago, this kind of research would have taken hours of hands-on work. Now, a significant part of it can be delegated to AI.

Of course, none of this guarantees a profitable trading strategy. But the way we research, test, and optimize trading systems is changing right before our eyes.

Absolutely mind-blowing. And I think we're only getting started.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Cool that the agent ran the whole loop without you, that's a real time saver. The thing I'd check is how many settings it tried, since the screenshot shows a lot of passes and the top ones are often just the luckiest. Make sure the cross-validation used data the optimizer never saw, and see if the best settings still hold up when you nudge them a bit. Cymetica's Backtest Labs can keep the last 30% of history aside as out-of-sample, which is a simple way to do that check.

replies.author: EAForexLab

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good that you checked it yourself and shared that it failed OOS, most people skip that part. When you build the prompt system, I'd make the OOS test a hard rule the agent can't override, so any set that fails gets thrown out and not tweaked until it passes. I'd also have it log how many settings it tried, so you can see how lucky a good result might be.

comments.author: Xander-XGCS
comments.body:
Yeah as soon as vibecoding exploded, I realized designing singular strategies no longer made sense. So my team and I built a system based on our existing models that designs, back and forward tests, and will be releasing a limited API (potentially via subscription) for the best. 

https://xgcapitalstrategies.com/training-gym/

replies.author: EAForexLab
replies.body: Tell us more about this. What functionality do you have?

replies.author: Xander-XGCS
replies.body:
Well as of right now it takes the proprietary research developed over the past ten years that has to do with how we let each candidate model (small CNNs, LSTMs, other architectures - some deterministic) perceive the market, give it standard market data to compare, and potentially other datasets depending on what we wish to test, and set it to work it's way through that parameter space under certain constraints in an automated fashion looking for successful trading strategies. As of right now, we are mostly developing large, portfolio rebalancing strategies across hundreds or thousands of assets at a time.

I originally built it to save tokens as compared to having the coding agents run the tests themselves, and it turned into something that would be highly inefficient to have an agent run on its own (though MCP controls are being implemented). Once we had the deterministic system defined, we just let it run and find strategies faster than we ever could by hand or even with coding agents. Maybe running a very large agent swarm would be faster, but I don't have OpenAI levels of credits lol. Mind you, we do have some pretty powerful on prem hardware. This wouldn't run on just any laptop - not quickly anyways).

I figure the methodology could be adapted to other types of research as well that have large parameter search spaces.

comments.body: Cool workflow, and the hard part is exactly what you said: "problems with the results". A few thousand passes with profit factors in the teens on \~90 trades is what overfitting looks like, and an agent checking its own cross-validation won't catch that. What helped us: keep the last stretch of data out of the optimisation completely, let the agent pick one setting, then run it on paper live for a few months before real money. Also log every pass it threw away, not just the winner, so you can see how lucky the winner had to be.

comments.author: OutrageousDemands
comments.body:
I have a very similar setup I have been using for a while. 

I have 19 assets I like to trade, I start with a simple genetic optimisation of a theory across multiple timeframes to find potential candidates. I work on simple is better so rarely more than 1 input and exit logic constraints. Potential candidates are then taken forward for out of sample, parameter sensitivity, and monte Carlo Sim. My PC just chugs away generating potential strategies for me day and night without any input or oversight from me. I've got hundreds of potential strategies which I build portfolios from, from millions of tested setups (always amazes me how few successful looking strategies don't actually pass some even basic robustness testing!)

It's a game changer for retail, but over time more and more people will pick up on this. I think the main thing it has shown me is how few strategies maintain an 'edge' (if indeed it was ever there and not just statistical noise) so how important it is to run portfolios of strategies.

Trading or setup wise?

I have markdown files set up with full instructions and guides written by me and Argon, then just use a cheap model (flash 3.8) to actually manage executing headless running of the MT5 terminal. It has access to Dropbox folders with full read/write permissions so just accumulates everything there. When I set up a VPS to trade a prop firm challenge on, I just allow a single Dropbox folder to sync with the VPS that has everything needed as an output. I then have a simple 1 page website setup which I shortcut to on my phone to review progress and live challenges all on 1 page, and remote control anti-gravity from my phone, so I very rarely need to fully sit at the PC. comments.author: Distinct_Excuse2648
comments.body:
Great post, a few questions:  
1. How many parameter combinations did the agent test, and how did you correct for picking the best one by luck?  
2. What was the cross-validation exactly: walk-forward on unseen years, or k-fold on shuffled data?  
3. How did the chosen settings do on a period the agent never saw during optimization?  
4. With only 70-96 trades per pass, how stable are the results if you change a parameter slightly?  
5. Are spread, commission and slippage included in the backtest?  
6. Has it been run live or on a demo account yet, and how does live compare to the backtest?  
7. Did the agent ever reject a strategy as overfit on its own, or does it always return a best result?

replies.author: EAForexLab
replies.body:
Thank you for your comment.

1. Initially, the agent ran the parameters and identified those that had the greatest impact on the result. After that, it ran optimization on 10 parameters with different increments. As you can imagine, there were a lot of combinations. For this, it used a genetic algorithm.
2. Step-by-step testing for unknown periods.
3. Poor performance due to over-optimization.
4. Not tested.
5. Spread and commission were included during optimization.
6. There's no point in testing on a demo account yet, as stable parameters haven't been found.
7. Yes, it's even overly critical 😅

replies.author: Distinct_Excuse2648
replies.body: Thanks for the honest answers. One tip from our own testing: instead of searching 10 parameters at once, fix the rule before the test and change only 1-2 things at a time. Then a change counts only if it beats the current version on unseen data in both halves of the period, after costs, and over several runs with different random seeds (our results swing a lot just from luck). Most "improvements" we tried failed this, but the few that passed held up. Fewer parameters, stricter test.

comments.author: fleatedplutmting
comments.body:
The real breakthrough here isn't AI generating trading strategies. It's dramatically reducing the cost and time required to research, test and refine them.

What previously required programming expertise and hours of manual analysis is becoming accessible to virtually anyone with a hypothesis worth testing.

The important distinction is between finding a strategy that performs well on historical data and one that survives live market conditions. Overfitting, transaction costs, slippage and changing market regimes can quickly destroy impressive backtesting results.

The next big leap will be AI systems that don't just optimise strategies, but continuously challenge their own assumptions and recognise when an edge has disappeared.

That's when things get really interesting for algorithmic trading imo

comments.author: Ok_Map5721
comments.body:
Cool setup, genuinely. But look at the screenshot from the other side for a second.

That optimizer ran a few thousand passes, and the top results have 70 to 96 trades each. With that many tries and that few trades, some of them will look great purely by luck. The agent then picks the best ones and cross-validates, which helps, but only if the validation data was never touched during any of those passes.

And the part that worries me most is "the issues can be fixed by refining the prompts." Every refinement is another round of trying things until it looks good. An agent that iterates while you're at the gym doesn't remove overfitting, it does it faster and without you watching.

What would make this genuinely powerful is giving the agent the boring rules too: count every pass it ran, correct the result for that number (deflated Sharpe is a good start), keep a holdout it's never allowed to see until the very end, and make it report the minimum trade count needed for the result to mean anything. If it can do that on its own, then I'll agree it's a new era.

replies.author: Ester_77
replies.body: Nice breakdown. The point about how many passes the optimizer ran is an easy one to overlook

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: Thanks. A rough rule of thumb that made it click for me: if you try N strategies that are all pure noise, the best one will typically show a t-stat around sqrt(2 × ln N). For 1,000 passes that's about 3.7. For 5,000 it's about 4.1. So a "significant" t of 2 or 3 out of an optimizer run is exactly what luck looks like.
